title: Saif Ali Khan Touched His Own Poster, Pumped His Fist, and Accidentally Created the Best Meme of the Week
excerpt: Between a viral blessing moment, an Amul topical, and Netflix's grittiest cop drama this year, 'Kartavya' is having the strangest promotional run in recent Bollywood memory
body:
Saif Ali Khan has done many things in his three-decade career — reinvented himself as an action star, married into Bollywood royalty, grown a beard that became a national conversation. But nothing in his filmography prepared him for what happened this week: he touched his own movie poster, pumped his fist, and the internet decided it was the funniest thing they'd seen all month.

The Moment That Launched a Thousand Memes

The clip is barely five seconds long. Saif, at a promotional event for Kartavya, walks up to the film's poster, places his hand on it — almost reverentially, the way you'd touch a temple idol — and then does a small, triumphant fist pump. It was spontaneous. It was sincere. And it was immediately, devastatingly meme-able.

Within hours, the clip had been remixed with everything from cricket commentary ("And Saif reviews his own innings!") to office-meeting energy ("When your own presentation slide looks fire"). Saif himself addressed it with the kind of self-aware humour that's become his signature: he admitted the gesture was purely instinctive, not self-congratulatory, and said he's happy the internet found it entertaining.

"I touched the poster and felt something," he told reporters, laughing. "Apparently, so did Twitter."

Amul Jumped In (Obviously)

You know a moment has crossed into the cultural mainstream when Amul makes a topical about it. The dairy giant's latest cartoon features a Saif-like figure touching a giant butter pack with the tagline "Kartavya — Utterly Devoted!" Kareena Kapoor Khan reshared it on her Instagram stories with a string of laughing emojis and a simple caption: "My husband, ladies and gentlemen."

It's the kind of organic promotional cycle that PR teams spend crores trying to manufacture — and Saif got it by being genuinely, endearingly himself.

But What About the Actual Film?

Beneath the meme chaos, Kartavya is a legitimate film that landed on Netflix on May 15 and deserves conversation beyond its promotional antics. Directed by Pulkit, it casts Saif as Pawan Malik, a morally conflicted police officer in a fictional Haryanvi town, investigating a journalist's assassination that pulls him into a web of caste politics, honour killings, and systemic corruption.

The reviews are split in a way that's become familiar for Saif's more ambitious projects. Critics praise his restrained, career-best performance — the kind of simmering intensity he last brought to Sacred Games. Rasika Dugal and Sanjay Mishra are singled out as exceptional. The film's visual restraint, all dusty roads and fluorescent-lit police stations, gives it a documentary grit that sets it apart from Netflix India's glossier offerings.

Where reviewers diverge is on the writing. Several critics call the plot "formulaic" and "predictable," drawing comparisons to Kohrra (Netflix's 2023 Haryanvi crime drama) without matching its raw emotional impact. Others argue that the social commentary — particularly around caste and institutional complicity — gives it substance that outlasts its narrative weaknesses.

The NRI Streaming Verdict

For diaspora audiences, Kartavya is the kind of Netflix drop that works perfectly for a weekend evening: dark enough to feel substantial, star-powered enough to hold your attention, and — at roughly two hours — mercifully free of the bloat that plagues many Indian OTT releases. It's streaming globally, so NRIs in the US, UK, and Canada can judge the meme-poster moment and the film on the same platform.

The consensus from early NRI social media chatter: watch it for Saif, stay for Rasika Dugal, and keep your expectations calibrated somewhere between Sacred Games and a solid prime-time police procedural.

Saif Ali Khan may have accidentally created 2026's most relatable meme. But he also quietly delivered one of the year's more interesting Hindi performances. As usual with Saif, the serious stuff gets buried under the noise — and as usual, it's worth finding.
